source.title: Applying Differential Learning During Rehabilitation After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: A Basketball Single-Case Study

paper.citation: Arede, J., Zhou, R., Singh, H., & Schöllhorn, W. I. (2025). Applying differential learning during rehabilitation after anterior cruciate ligament injury: A basketball single-case study. Healthcare, 13(24), 3247. https://doi.org/10.3390/healthcare13243247
paper.abstract: Is it feasible to integrate differential-learning principles across a structured ACL-reconstruction rehabilitation, and how did one basketball player's function, performance, and psychological readiness change? Participant: One 18-year-old male trained amateur basketball player with 12 years of basketball and 5 years of resistance-training experience. Injury: Complete left ACL tear treated with reconstruction using a patellar-tendon allograft. Training or return-to-play context: Forty-two weeks spanning pre-operative, early, mid, late, return-to-training, and return-to-play phases. Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: Single successful case with satisfactory adherence and no major complications; it does not represent the range of ACL grafts, concomitant injuries, setbacks, ages, sexes, or sport contexts. Design: Prospective single-case description without a control condition. Exposure or intervention: Conventional criterion-based rehabilitation plus differential-learning variations in geometry, velocity, acceleration, and rhythm across mobility, strength, plyometric, running, and basketball-specific tasks. Comparator: Pre-injury monitoring values, serial within-athlete values, contralateral limb, and published reference thresholds. Measurements and outcomes: Daily IKDC, end-point ACL-RSI and Knee Outcome Survey, hop asymmetry, strength, change of direction, sprinting, session RPE, sleep, HRV, resting heart rate, and total quality recovery. Analysis: ARIMA, breakpoint, and segmented-regression analyses of repeated IKDC scores, plus descriptive performance comparisons.
paper.tldr: This longitudinal single case gives a detailed, criterion-based example of integrating differential-learning variations throughout ACL reconstruction rehabilitation and basketball return to sport. The player returned to competition at the pre-injury level after 33 days of unrestricted team training, playing 32 minutes in a low-difficulty game his team won by 31 points. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Design: Prospective single-case description without a control condition. Exposure or intervention: Conventional criterion-based rehabilitation plus differential-learning variations in geometry, velocity, acceleration, and rhythm across mobility, strength, plyometric, running, and basketball-specific tasks. Comparator: Pre-injury monitoring values, serial within-athlete values, contralateral limb, and published reference thresholds. Measurements and outcomes: Daily IKDC, end-point ACL-RSI and Knee Outcome Survey, hop asymmetry, strength, change of direction, sprinting, session RPE, sleep, HRV, resting heart rate, and total quality recovery. Analysis: ARIMA, breakpoint, and segmented-regression analyses of repeated IKDC scores, plus descriptive performance comparisons.
paper.findings: The player returned to competition at the pre-injury level after 33 days of unrestricted team training, playing 32 minutes in a low-difficulty game his team won by 31 points. IKDC increased from 13.8% at baseline to 95.4% at return to play; ACL-RSI was 85.2%, the daily-living score was 95.7%, and single- and triple-hop asymmetries were below 10%. The segmented model of IKDC scores explained 96.0% of variance and identified a rapid early rise, a brief decline around days 23–25, and later stabilized improvement. At return to play, maximum strength, agility, and sprint performance were reported as better than pre-injury values.
paper.limitations: With one participant and no concurrent comparison, recovery cannot be attributed to differential learning separately from surgery, conventional rehabilitation, natural healing, training dose, monitoring, motivation, or support. End-point limb symmetry and pre-injury comparisons do not establish restored movement quality, reinjury protection, or long-term competition durability. Dense repeated IKDC scores increase observations but not independent participants; model fit describes this trajectory and does not validate a general recovery phase structure. Some thresholds were used both to progress rehabilitation and describe success, which makes them clinical decision criteria rather than independent evidence of efficacy. The authors explicitly limit generalizability and recommend larger randomized comparisons, quantified movement variability, electromyography, and motion capture.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the phase structure and movement-variation examples as a case-informed design library, not evidence that differential learning improves ACL outcomes. Preserve criterion-based progression, graft and tissue-healing constraints, basketball exposure, psychological readiness, and medical oversight. If adopted, prospectively define adherence, symptoms, objective performance, movement quality, competition exposure, and adverse outcomes.
